name: Submalar filler

lead: Submalar filler adds volume to the hollow beneath the cheekbones, giving a fuller or more defined lower midface and a lifted cheek contour. The change is visible after treatment.

It is a non-surgical counterpart to submalar implants, which augment the midface while malar implants sit on the cheekbones. A clinician injects a gel filler, typically hyaluronic acid, into the tissue below the cheekbone, adding volume until the body gradually resorbs it. Small registered trials have tested hyaluronic acid and other fillers for midface volume and cheek augmentation.

paras: It is a short clinic treatment with little downtime. People choose it as a temporary, reversible way to try a fuller cheek contour, and repeat it as the filler is absorbed.
Asymmetry from uneven resorption or shifting is listed among the risks of cheek augmentation. Filler is eventually resorbed, so results are temporary. Fillers are given by licensed practitioners.

angle.text: Submalar filler adds volume in the hollow beneath the cheekbone for a fuller, lifted cheek contour, as a non-surgical counterpart to submalar implants. The change is visible after treatment and is temporary. Small registered trials have tested fillers for midface volume.

lead: Submalar filler is a gel dermal filler, usually hyaluronic acid, injected in the hollow below the cheekbone to add volume to the lower midface. People use it to get a fuller, more lifted-looking cheek, soften a gaunt or sunken look beneath the cheekbones and create a smoother transition from cheek to jaw without surgery.[1][2]

It is the injectable counterpart of the submalar implant. Wikipedia describes submalar implants as sitting below rather than on the cheekbones, augmenting the midface especially for a gaunt or sunken look, whereas malar implants sit on the cheekbones for a higher contour.[1] Fillers are less invasive and less expensive than implants, but they are eventually resorbed, with fat described as more permanent.[1]

Dermal fillers in general last for about six months according to Wikipedia, depending on filler type, skin health, provider skill and activity in the area.[2] Registered clinical trials of mid-face volume fillers are under way or completed.[3][4]
infobox: Eventually resorbed; about six months for many fillers[1][2]

paras: Wikipedia describes cheek augmentation as done with implants (silicone, porous polyethylene or ePTFE) or with injectables, and distinguishes malar implants (cheekbones), submalar implants (midface) and combined implants. Fillers are injected rather than implanted, and fat, although described as more permanent, is still resorbed.[1]

Dermal filler types include hyaluronic acid, most commonly cross-linked with BDDE for stability, other natural polymers such as collagen, and synthetic polymers. Fillers are used for wrinkles and folds, age-related volume loss and contours of the lips, cheeks and jawline.[2]

Wikipedia states the effect of dermal fillers lasts about six months and some people need more than one injection, with duration depending on skin health, provider skill, filler type and activity in the injected area; exercise and manual labor can shorten it.[2]
For cheek augmentation, Wikipedia lists asymmetry from uneven resorption or shifting as a risk, and temporary loss of sensation as common with implants.[1]

For dermal fillers, common effects are bruising, redness, pain and itching; less commonly infections and allergic reactions that can cause lumps or scarring. Rare serious complications include blindness from retrograde embolization into the ophthalmic and retinal arteries, and delayed skin necrosis, with embolic complications more frequent with autologous fat, followed by hyaluronic acid.[2]

A registered study of a hyaluronic acid product for restoration of mid-face volume deficit in 30 participants began recruiting in January 2025.[3] A small completed study of the tissue filler SMI-01 in the nasolabial fold and cheek augmentation enrolled 21 participants and started in November 2020.[4] Results are not summarised in the registry entries.

timeline.event: Study of SMI-01 tissue filler for nasolabial fold and cheek augmentation begins (n=21).[4]
Study of a hyaluronic acid product for mid-face volume deficit begins recruiting (n=30).[3]
